# Pre-Phase-5 Cleanup + Prep

Phase 4 shipped in full (slice 4.8, PR #31, merged 2026-07-18). Before Phase 5
(musl + file systems) starts, the close-out review identified a set of
PR-sized cleanup/prep chunks so Phase 5 does not build on soft ground.

**How to use this file:** each chunk is one session / one PR. Chunks 1–5 and 7
were independent and could land in any order; chunk 6 (the Phase 5 design +
slicing session) must come last — it gates starting Phase 5 proper (chunk 7
did not gate Phase 5). **Chunk 6 is now the only chunk left.** Markers follow
the `docs/plan.md` convention: `◀ next` (unstarted), `◀ ready (branch …, pending
merge)`, `✓ shipped (PR #N, merged YYYY-MM-DD)`. Flip a chunk's marker as part
of its own PR, and move `◀ next` to whichever chunk you intend to take next.

---

## Chunk 1: CI QEMU smoke job ✓ shipped (PR #33, merged 2026-07-24)

**Goal:** the kernel's `target_os = "none"` modules currently have zero CI
coverage — every Phase 2–4 regression was caught by hand-running QEMU. One
smoke job closes that gap cheaply.

**Scope:**

- New job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (ubuntu): install
  `qemu-system-aarch64` + edk2 firmware, build the kernel
  (`cargo kernel-aarch64`), boot via the cargo runner under `timeout 25`,
  capture the serial log to a file.
- Grep the log (`grep -a` — raw tick bytes make it binary-ish) against a
  checked-in expected-substrings file (e.g. `tests/qemu-boot.expected`):
  the 11 `[as]` lines, init's `SYS_FORK`/`SYS_EXEC name=worker`/`SYS_EXIT`
  chain, stub D's designed `sig=11` kill chain, RS `[alarm]` fires; and
  assert the absence of `panic` / `el0_sync_unexpected`.
- Start `continue-on-error: true` like geiger/miri; flip to blocking once it
  proves stable across a few PRs.
- Remember QEMU-under-TCG guest time runs slower than wall clock — pick
  expectations that land well inside the timeout (boot chatter + first alarm
  fires, not tick counts).
- Pin any third-party actions to full commit SHAs (repo convention).

**Proof:** a PR that deliberately breaks boot (or the expected file) fails the
job; a green run greps every expected marker.

**Notes (investigation, resolved):** blog_os-style `custom_test_frameworks`
in-QEMU unit tests were evaluated and deliberately deferred. The approach
ports to aarch64 — the unstable feature is still live; QEMU exit works via a
semihosting `SYS_EXIT` (`HLT #0xF000`) plus
`-semihosting-config enable=on,target=native`, replacing x86's
`isa-debug-exit`; the `qemu-exit` / taiki-e `semihosting` crates are
MIT/Apache-2.0 — but it is the wrong tool for this chunk's assertion
(full-system serial-log properties, not per-function unit results) and would
not remove the kernel's `#[cfg(target_os = "none")]` gating either (see
chunk 7). Revisit as a future in-QEMU unit-test chunk.

## Chunk 2: mdBook content port + legacy docs retirement ✓ shipped (PR #34, merged 2026-07-24)

**Goal:** the mdBook in `book/` is the canonical documentation, but its
architecture/IPC pages are stubs while the real content sits in legacy
`docs/*.md` written in Phase-0 future tense (CoW, drivers, musl described as
present). Port with an accuracy pass; retire the legacy files.

**Scope:**

- Port `docs/{architecture,ipc,servers,boot,build,memory-layout,syscalls,
  drivers,musl,minix3-mapping}.md` into `book/src/` chapters, rewritten
  against source: present tense only for what exists as of Phase 4;
  aspirational content either dropped or clearly marked as roadmap.
- Delete each legacy `docs/*.md` as it is ported (`docs/plan.md` and
  `docs/plans/` stay — they are the planning tree, not the book).
- Document the QEMU trace-forensics rule in the book's build/debugging
  chapter (zero `[ipc]` samples ≠ stuck caller; head-carve vs modulo
  sampling; `grep -a`; TCG time skew) — currently tribal knowledge in
  CLAUDE.md only.
- May split into two PRs (kernel chapters first, servers/build second).

**Proof:** `mdbook build book` green; legacy files gone; book pages describe
only what boots today.

## Chunk 3: Stub A–D disable flag ✓ shipped (PR #35, merged 2026-07-24)

**Goal:** stubs A–D are the live regression battery (IPC ping-pong, SCHED
delegation, VM fault paths) but they consume ASIDs/priv slots and flood traces
(stub C especially). Debugging init/musl wants a clean boot without deleting
the battery.

**Scope:**

- Cargo feature on the kernel crate (e.g. `boot-stubs`, **default-on**)
  gating the stub blob assembly (`user_stub.S` in `build.rs`), the
  `build_stub` calls + VAs + priv installs in `userland.rs`, and PM's stub
  `mproc` seeds (PM must not seed procs that don't exist — check
  `com.rs`/`mproc.rs` coupling; `NR_STUB_PROCS` and `FORK_POOL_BASE` must
  stay consistent between the kernel and PM for a given feature setting).
- Default stays on so CI smoke (chunk 1) and normal dev keep the battery.
- Document the flag + the clean-boot invocation in CLAUDE.md and the book's
  build chapter.

**Proof:** `--no-default-features`-style boot shows only servers + init/worker
`[as]` lines and no stub traffic; default boot unchanged.

## Chunk 4: Capacity ceilings ✓ shipped (PR #36, merged 2026-07-24)

**Goal:** the effective user-process capacity is spread across three silent
constants — PM `NR_MPROCS` (32), VM `MAX_CLIENTS` (32), and the SCHED table
(16) — plus VM `MAX_REGIONS = 4` per client, which one loader + heap + stack
+ a few mmaps will blow immediately in Phase 5.

**Scope:**

- Raise VM `MAX_REGIONS` 4 → 16.
- Move the shared capacity story into `kernel-shared` (one constant for the
  user-process ceiling; PM/VM/SCHED tables sized from it) instead of three
  independent numbers that happen to agree.
- Const-assert the relationships (`MAX_CLIENTS >= NR_MPROCS`, fork pool fits,
  SCHED table covers delegated procs) so a future bump can't silently skew.

**Proof:** host tests green; QEMU boot + fork/exec loop unchanged; a
deliberate mismatched-constant build fails at compile time.

## Chunk 5: Toolchain bump + kernel clippy debt ✓ shipped (PR #37, merged 2026-07-24)

**Goal:** the pinned nightly (`rust-toolchain.toml`) is ~2 months old; bump it
deliberately *before* Phase 5 churn, not mid-slice. Same session: deal with
the known kernel-target clippy lints that CI never sees.

**Scope:**

- Bump the dated nightly pin; fix fmt/lint fallout across the workspace
  (blocking gates: `cargo fmt --all --check`,
  `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, plus
  `cargo kernel-aarch64` and the QEMU boot).
- Fix or explicitly quarantine (`#[allow]` + comment) the pre-existing
  `cargo clippy -p minixrs-kernel --target aarch64-unknown-none` lints
  (nomem-asm pointers, `manual_is_multiple_of`, interior-mutable-const).
- Optional: add a non-blocking CI job running kernel-target clippy so the
  surface stays visible.

**Proof:** all blocking gates green on the new nightly; kernel-target clippy
clean or every remaining lint carries an explicit allow + rationale.

## Chunk 6: Phase 5 design + slicing session (gates Phase 5) ◀ next

**Goal:** Phase 5 in `docs/plan.md` is six bullets and a milestone. Phases 2–4
succeeded because each slice was PR-sized, independently bootable, and left a
QEMU-visible trace. Phase 5 needs the same treatment — and several design
decisions locked *before* wrappers are written.

**Scope:** a dedicated brainstorm/design session (plan mode, not
implementation) producing `docs/plans/phase-5-musl-fs.md`:

- **Design decisions to lock:** console/stdio sink for the `printf` milestone
  (kernel diag call vs minimal TTY vs deferred); root-image strategy
  (initramfs vs MXBI-embedded FS image before block drivers); grant model
  (real MINIX-style safecopy grants vs interim kernel copy API — prefer real
  grants); ELF-loading authority for FS-backed exec (reuse kernel
  `boot_image/elf.rs` vs VM/PM); cbindgen/ABI-freeze timing for the
  `kernel-shared` → C header bridge; musl vendoring policy (tree vs
  submodule, CI scan exclusions).
- **Slice decomposition:** PR-sized slices with observable QEMU proof each.
  Expected opening slices (feature work, deliberately *not* in this cleanup
  file): fault-safe user copy for messages (`EFAULT`, not a kernel panic, on
  a bad user pointer) and a real grant table + `SYS_SAFECOPY`/`SYS_SETGRANT`
  — every interesting Phase 5 data path (VFS read/write, MFS↔VFS, later
  BDEV) moves bytes cross-address-space.
- Rewrite `docs/plan.md`'s Phase 5 section as the slice list and move
  `◀ next` onto slice 5.0.

**Proof:** the design doc exists with every decision above resolved (not
"TBD"), and plan.md's Phase 5 section is a slice table.

## Chunk 7: De-host the kernel crate ◀ ready (branch feature/dehost-kernel, pending merge)

**Goal:** every kernel module was `#[cfg(target_os = "none")]`-gated so host
workspace builds saw an empty crate — which is why kernel code was invisible to
the blocking lint gates. Remove the kernel crate from host builds entirely so
the per-item gates can go away.

**Scope** (the original bullets 2 and 3 were absorbed by chunk 5, which shipped
the `clippy-kernel` job and cleared the named lints; only bullet 1 remained,
plus the follow-through that job's own comment nominated):

- Stop host-building `minixrs-kernel` by pinning its target in its own manifest:
  `forced-target = "aarch64-unknown-none"` under
  `cargo-features = ["per-package-target"]`, plus `test = false`/`bench = false`
  on the bin (a `--test` build needs the `test` crate → `E0463`). Every cargo
  invocation then cross-compiles it — bare, `--workspace`, or from an IDE — and
  a host build is unreachable even with an explicit `--target`.
  - This replaced a first attempt that used workspace `default-members` +
    `--exclude minixrs-kernel` in CI. That worked for CI but broke RustRover,
    whose linter runs `cargo check --all-targets --workspace --features
    minixrs-kernel/…`; `--exclude` is rejected outright when features name the
    excluded package, so there was no one-setting IDE fix. A nested workspace
    (`exclude = ["kernel"]`) was also prototyped and rejected — it breaks the
    relative linker-script path in `.cargo/config.toml`, needs the release
    profile duplicated, a second committed `Cargo.lock`, and extra
    `fmt`/`audit`/`deny` CI invocations.
  - Cost accepted: `per-package-target` is unstable (cargo#9406), contained by
    the dated nightly pin and failing loudly (manifest error) if ever dropped.
    It also overrides `--target` in an alias, so the `kernel-x86_64` alias is
    removed; Phase 8 must relax `forced-target` before restoring it.
  - CI's `clippy`/`coverage` keep `--exclude minixrs-kernel` for runner cost
    (clang cross-assembly + 8 nested server builds on an x86 blocking gate),
    and `geiger`'s per-package sweep filters it out. A local
    `cargo clippy --workspace` *does* lint kernel code — the blind spot is
    closed, not relocated.
- Drop all 15 `cfg(target_os = "none")` gates from `kernel/src/main.rs`
  (unconditional `no_std`/`no_main`, no host `fn main() {}` fallback). Two
  guards make an accidental host build one clear message: `build.rs` emits
  `cargo::error=` before rustc runs, and `main.rs` carries a `compile_error!`
  mirroring `arch/mod.rs`'s arch guard.
- Flip `clippy-kernel` to **blocking** — with the kernel out of every host gate
  it is the only CI job that compiles kernel code at all — and give it a second
  `--no-default-features` run so chunk 3's stub-free config is guarded too.
- Flip `qemu-smoke` to **blocking** (green across PRs #33–#37, satisfying
  chunk 1's "stable across a few PRs" bar) and require its boot step to exit 124.
- Drive-by: `user_va_ok` + `USER_VA_TOP` and their 5 tests move from
  `kernel/src/ipc/message.rs` to `kernel-shared/src/message.rs`. The tests had
  never executed (the module was cfg-gated out on host); de-hosting would have
  made that permanent. `kernel-shared` goes 49 → 54 running tests, and
  `arch/aarch64/addrspace.rs`'s duplicate `USER_VA_TOP` literal folds in.

**Proof:** host gates green with the kernel excluded; `cargo check --workspace`
fails with exactly one actionable error; `cargo kernel-aarch64` and both QEMU
boots (default + stub-free) unchanged; kernel-target clippy blocking in CI.

---

## Drive-by notes (not chunks)

- Stale era comments ("until phase 3", "slice 2.6+") in
  `kernel/src/ipc/{message.rs,senda.rs,mod.rs}` hot paths — clean up in the
  first Phase 5 PR that touches those files; not worth a standalone PR.
- README / book "six IPC primitives" claims were softened to "five live +
  SENDA stubbed" in the close-out PR; if SENDA ever becomes real (it is
  currently `ENOSYS` *and* denied by the `trap_mask: u16` gate — bit 16
  doesn't fit), restore the claim then.

## Non-goals before Phase 5

Do **not** block Phase 5 on: the x86_64 port (Phase 8), VirtIO blk/net
(Phase 6 — only a console story is needed for the printf milestone), CoW
fork, full RS live-update/restart, implementing SENDA, an interactive
shell/coreutils (Phase 7), replacing stubs A–D entirely (the disable flag is
enough), or full POSIX signal semantics (DFL/IGN + kill + wait first;
handlers follow).

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## plugin:github:github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kevinbarnard/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

1	# minix.rs: Implementation Plan
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	Build minix.rs as a learning OS that preserves MINIX 3's microkernel architecture -- message-passing IPC, user-space servers (PM, VFS, VM, RS, DS, SCHED), user-space drivers, and fine-grained privilege control -- but with a greenfield Rust kernel targeting modern 64-bit platforms (x86_64, aarch64) under QEMU/VirtIO. Someone familiar with MINIX 3 or the Tanenbaum book should recognize the concepts immediately.
6	
7	**Key constraints:**
8	- BSD/MIT licensing only (no GPL)
9	- musl-libc fork for MINIX syscall wrappers
10	- aarch64 first (native Apple Silicon dev platform), then x86_64
11	- QEMU as primary platform, VirtIO drivers
12	- Custom basic userland (not NetBSD)
13	
14	**Reference material:**
15	- MINIX 3 source (architectural reference only): https://github.com/Stichting-MINIX-Research-Foundation/minix
16	- musl-libc upstream: https://musl.libc.org/ (fork v1.2.5 for MINIX adaptation)
17	- Limine bootloader: https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Architecture Overview
22	
23	```
24	+------------------------------------------------------------------+

202	## Core Data Structures (Rust)

207	/// 104-byte fixed-size IPC message matching MINIX 3 x86_64 layout.
208	#[repr(C)]
209	#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
210	pub struct Message {
211	    pub m_source: Endpoint,    // Who sent this (set by kernel)
212	    pub m_type: i32,           // Call number or result code
213	    pub payload: [u8; 96],     // Typed access via accessor methods
214	}
215	```
216	
217	Typed message accessors (e.g., `msg.as_vfs_read()`) replace MINIX 3's opaque `m1i1`/`m2l1` field names -- a major educational improvement. The `kernel-shared` crate provides both the raw `Message` and typed accessor structs for each call.
218	
219	### Process Table (kernel)
220	
221	```rust
222	pub const NR_TASKS: usize = 5;     // ASYNCM, IDLE, CLOCK, SYSTEM, HARDWARE
223	pub const NR_PROCS: usize = 1024;
224	
225	pub struct Proc {
226	    pub regs: ArchRegisterFrame,
227	    pub nr: ProcNr,
228	    pub endpoint: Endpoint,
229	    pub priv_ptr: Option<PrivId>,   // Index into privilege table
230	    pub rts_flags: AtomicU32,       // RTS_SENDING | RTS_RECEIVING | ...
231	    pub misc_flags: u32,            // MF_DELIVERMSG | ...
232	    pub priority: u8,
233	    pub quantum_left: u64,
234	
235	    // IPC state -- linked lists via indices, not raw pointers
236	    pub caller_q: Option<ProcNr>,   // Head of callers wanting to send to us
237	    pub q_link: Option<ProcNr>,     // Next in caller queue
238	    pub getfrom_e: Endpoint,        // Whom we're waiting to receive from
239	    pub sendto_e: Endpoint,         // Whom we're waiting to send to
240	    pub send_msg: Message,          // Buffered outgoing message
241	    pub deliver_msg: Message,       // Message to deliver on unblock
242	
243	    pub name: [u8; 16],
244	}
245	```
246	
247	Using `Option<ProcNr>` (table indices) instead of raw pointers for linked lists eliminates aliasing hazards and makes the code safer and easier to reason about.
248	
249	### Privilege Structure (kernel)
250	
251	```rust
252	pub struct Priv {
253	    pub id: SysId,
254	    pub flags: u16,                              // PREEMPTIBLE, BILLABLE
255	    pub trap_mask: u16,                           // Allowed IPC traps bitmap
256	    pub ipc_to: [u32; NR_SYS_PROCS / 32],       // Allowed IPC destinations
257	    pub k_call_mask: [u32; NR_SYS_CALLS / 32],  // Allowed kernel calls
258	    pub notify_pending: [u32; NR_SYS_PROCS / 32],
259	    pub io_ranges: ArrayVec<IoRange, 16>,
260	    pub irqs: ArrayVec<u32, 8>,
261	    pub grant_table: VirAddr,
262	    pub grant_entries: usize,
263	}
264	```

267	
268	## IPC Semantics (preserved from MINIX 3)
269	
270	Six primitives, same semantics as MINIX 3's `proc.c`:
271	
272	| Primitive | Behavior |
273	|-----------|----------|
274	| `SEND`    | Block until receiver accepts message |
275	| `RECEIVE` | Block until a message arrives (checks notify pending, async pending, caller queue) |
276	| `SENDREC` | Atomic SEND + RECEIVE (most common -- used by `_syscall()`) |
277	| `NOTIFY`  | Set bit in receiver's `notify_pending` bitmap; non-blocking |
278	| `SENDNB`  | Non-blocking send; returns error if receiver not waiting |
279	| `SENDA`   | Process table of async messages |
280	
281	**Entry path (aarch64):** User executes `SVC #0`. Exception vector saves registers, calls `do_ipc()` in Rust.
282	
283	**Entry path (x86_64):** User executes `SYSCALL` instruction. Kernel entry in `entry.S` saves registers, calls same `do_ipc()`.
284	
285	---
286	
287	## System Call Path (same as MINIX 3)
288	
289	```
290	User: read(fd, buf, count)
291	  |
292	  v
293	musl: read.c fills Message { m_type: VFS_READ, fd, buf_ptr, count }
294	  |   calls _syscall(VFS_PROC_NR, VFS_READ, &msg)
295	  |     calls ipc_sendrec(VFS_PROC_NR, &msg)
296	  |       executes SVC (aarch64) or SYSCALL (x86_64)
297	  v
298	Kernel: do_ipc() -> mini_send() copies msg to VFS deliver_msg, unblocks VFS
299	         -> mini_receive() blocks caller until VFS replies
300	  |
301	  v
302	VFS: sef_receive() returns the message
303	  |   dispatches to do_read()
304	  |   routes to MFS via REQ_READ message
305	  |   MFS reads from disk (via BDEV_READ to virtio-blk)
306	  |   MFS replies to VFS
307	  |   VFS replies to user process
308	  v
309	Kernel: mini_send() delivers reply, unblocks user
310	  |
311	  v
312	musl: _syscall() returns result, sets errno if negative
313	  |
314	  v
315	User: read() returns bytes read
316	```
317	
318	---
319	
320	## musl-libc Integration
321	
322	The musl fork (v1.2.5, MIT license) needs the following changes:
323	
324	**New files to add (`src/minix/`):**
325	- `_syscall.c` -- `int _syscall(endpoint_t who, int callnr, message *m)` using `ipc_sendrec()`
326	- `_ipc_aarch64.S` -- `SVC`-based IPC trap
327	- `_ipc_x86_64.S` -- `SYSCALL`-based IPC trap (matches kernel's `entry.S` ABI)
328	- ~100 POSIX wrapper files (open.c, read.c, write.c, fork.c, exit.c, etc.) that construct MINIX messages and call `_syscall()`. Structurally identical to MINIX 3's `lib/libc/sys/` wrappers.
329	
330	**Files to modify:**
331	- `arch/aarch64/syscall_arch.h` -- Gut Linux `__syscall*` macros; redirect to MINIX path
332	- `arch/x86_64/syscall_arch.h` -- Same
333	- `Makefile` -- Add `src/minix/` sources
334	
335	**Include bridge:** A small header set (`minix/ipc.h`, `minix/com.h`, `minix/callnr.h`) generated from `kernel-shared` Rust crate via `cbindgen`, so the C wrappers use the same message types and call numbers as the Rust kernel and servers.

337	---
338	
339	## Boot Sequence
340	
341	**Bootloader:** Limine (BSD-licensed, supports x86_64 BIOS+UEFI and aarch64 UEFI).
342	
343	```
344	Limine loads kernel ELF64 from FAT32 boot partition
345	  -> _start (entry.S): set kernel stack, call kmain()
346	  -> kmain():
347	     1. Parse Limine responses (memmap, HHDM offset)
348	     2. Init kernel heap, serial console
349	     3. Unpack embedded boot image -> module_list[]
350	     4. arch_init() -- exception vectors, GIC, timer (aarch64) or GDT/IDT/APIC (x86_64)
351	     5. proc_init() -- clear process table
352	     6. Load each boot module ELF, create page tables, set privileges
353	     7. system_init() -- register kernel call handlers
354	     8. Enable timer interrupt
355	     9. Unblock boot processes
356	    10. switch_to_user() -- schedule first process (never returns)
357	
358	Boot processes start in order:
359	  DS -> RS -> PM -> SCHED -> VFS -> memory -> tty -> VM -> PFS -> MFS -> init
360	```
361	
362	Boot modules are packed into the kernel ELF as a `.boot_image` section (MXBI header + ELF entries).

371	- **`tools/mkbootimage.rs`** packs server/driver ELF binaries into the boot archive linked into the kernel
372	- **`tools/mkimage.sh`** creates GPT disk: FAT32 boot partition (Limine + kernel) + MinixFS root
373	- **`tools/qemu-run.sh`** launches QEMU with VirtIO devices and serial console

564	## Key Design Decisions
565	
566	**Rust kernel, not incremental port:** MINIX 3's C kernel uses raw pointers, global mutable state, and macro-heavy abstractions that resist incremental Rustification. A greenfield kernel uses proper Rust patterns from the start (enums for flags, Result for errors, indices not pointers for linked lists).
567	
568	**`unsafe` boundaries in kernel:** (a) Process table access (`UnsafeCell` static array), (b) user-space memory copies, (c) hardware register access (inline asm), (d) assembly entry/exit paths. Each `unsafe` block gets a `// SAFETY:` comment.
569	
570	**musl over Rust libc:** musl is well-tested, BSD-compatible, and complete. The MINIX-specific work is confined to ~100 syscall wrappers + IPC assembly stub. The rest of musl (stdio, string, math, locale) works unchanged.
571	
572	**Servers in Rust:** Shared `kernel-shared` message types provide compile-time IPC protocol verification. C servers (linked against musl) also work since the IPC mechanism is language-agnostic.
573	
574	**Multi-call coreutils:** Single `coreutils` binary dispatching on argv[0] (like BusyBox) minimizes disk space and simplifies building.

588	- Phase 6: Boots from VirtIO disk, mounts MinixFS root
589	- Phase 7: Interactive shell session

591	- Phase 9: `cargo doc`, test suite green

598	  -device virtio-net-device
599	```
600	GDB: add `-s -S` then `rust-gdb -ex "target remote :1234"`
601	
602	---
603	
604	## Critical Reference Files (MINIX 3)

# minix.rs: Implementation Plan

## Context

Build minix.rs as a learning OS that preserves MINIX 3's microkernel architecture -- message-passing IPC, user-space servers (PM, VFS, VM, RS, DS, SCHED), user-space drivers, and fine-grained privilege control -- but with a greenfield Rust kernel targeting modern 64-bit platforms (x86_64, aarch64) under QEMU/VirtIO. Someone familiar with MINIX 3 or the Tanenbaum book should recognize the concepts immediately.

**Key constraints:**
- BSD/MIT licensing only (no GPL)
- musl-libc fork for MINIX syscall wrappers
- aarch64 first (native Apple Silicon dev platform), then x86_64
- QEMU as primary platform, VirtIO drivers
- Custom basic userland (not NetBSD)

**Reference material:**
- MINIX 3 source (architectural reference only): https://github.com/Stichting-MINIX-Research-Foundation/minix
- musl-libc upstream: https://musl.libc.org/ (fork v1.2.5 for MINIX adaptation)
- Limine bootloader: https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine

## Architecture Overview

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        User Programs                             |
|  (linked against musl-minix, POSIX-compatible)                   |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
         |  _syscall(endpoint, callnr, &msg)  via SYSCALL/SVC
         v
+--------+--------+---------+--------+--------+--------+-----------+
|   PM   |  VFS   |   VM    |   RS   |   DS   | SCHED  | Drivers   |
| fork   | open   | mmap    | monitor| pub/   | policy | virtio-blk|
| exec   | read   | pageflt | restart| sub    |        | virtio-net|
| exit   | write  | brk     | live-  | store  |        | virtio-con|
| signal | close  | CoW     | update |        |        | memory    |
+--------+--------+---------+--------+--------+--------+-----------+
         |  IPC messages (SEND/RECEIVE/SENDREC/NOTIFY)
         v
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     minix.rs Microkernel (Rust)                  |
|  IPC | Scheduling | Interrupt dispatch | Memory protection       |
|  Kernel calls (SYS_*) for privileged servers                     |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  aarch64 HAL (primary)  |        x86_64 HAL                      |
|  SVC/ERET               |        SYSCALL/SYSRET                  |
|  GIC, translation tables|        APIC, 4-level PT                |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     Limine Bootloader                            |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

## Core Data Structures (Rust)

### Message (kernel-shared)

```rust
/// 104-byte fixed-size IPC message matching MINIX 3 x86_64 layout.
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
pub struct Message {
    pub m_source: Endpoint,    // Who sent this (set by kernel)
    pub m_type: i32,           // Call number or result code
    pub payload: [u8; 96],     // Typed access via accessor methods
}
```

Typed message accessors (e.g., `msg.as_vfs_read()`) replace MINIX 3's opaque `m1i1`/`m2l1` field names -- a major educational improvement. The `kernel-shared` crate provides both the raw `Message` and typed accessor structs for each call.

### Process Table (kernel)

```rust
pub const NR_TASKS: usize = 5;     // ASYNCM, IDLE, CLOCK, SYSTEM, HARDWARE
pub const NR_PROCS: usize = 1024;

pub struct Proc {
    pub regs: ArchRegisterFrame,
    pub nr: ProcNr,
    pub endpoint: Endpoint,
    pub priv_ptr: Option<PrivId>,   // Index into privilege table
    pub rts_flags: AtomicU32,       // RTS_SENDING | RTS_RECEIVING | ...
    pub misc_flags: u32,            // MF_DELIVERMSG | ...
    pub priority: u8,
    pub quantum_left: u64,

    // IPC state -- linked lists via indices, not raw pointers
    pub caller_q: Option<ProcNr>,   // Head of callers wanting to send to us
    pub q_link: Option<ProcNr>,     // Next in caller queue
    pub getfrom_e: Endpoint,        // Whom we're waiting to receive from
    pub sendto_e: Endpoint,         // Whom we're waiting to send to
    pub send_msg: Message,          // Buffered outgoing message
    pub deliver_msg: Message,       // Message to deliver on unblock

    pub name: [u8; 16],
}
```

Using `Option<ProcNr>` (table indices) instead of raw pointers for linked lists eliminates aliasing hazards and makes the code safer and easier to reason about.

### Privilege Structure (kernel)

```rust
pub struct Priv {
    pub id: SysId,
    pub flags: u16,                              // PREEMPTIBLE, BILLABLE
    pub trap_mask: u16,                           // Allowed IPC traps bitmap
    pub ipc_to: [u32; NR_SYS_PROCS / 32],       // Allowed IPC destinations
    pub k_call_mask: [u32; NR_SYS_CALLS / 32],  // Allowed kernel calls
    pub notify_pending: [u32; NR_SYS_PROCS / 32],
    pub io_ranges: ArrayVec<IoRange, 16>,
    pub irqs: ArrayVec<u32, 8>,
    pub grant_table: VirAddr,
    pub grant_entries: usize,
}
```

## IPC Semantics (preserved from MINIX 3)

Six primitives, same semantics as MINIX 3's `proc.c`:

| Primitive | Behavior |
|-----------|----------|
| `SEND`    | Block until receiver accepts message |
| `RECEIVE` | Block until a message arrives (checks notify pending, async pending, caller queue) |
| `SENDREC` | Atomic SEND + RECEIVE (most common -- used by `_syscall()`) |
| `NOTIFY`  | Set bit in receiver's `notify_pending` bitmap; non-blocking |
| `SENDNB`  | Non-blocking send; returns error if receiver not waiting |
| `SENDA`   | Process table of async messages |

**Entry path (aarch64):** User executes `SVC #0`. Exception vector saves registers, calls `do_ipc()` in Rust.

**Entry path (x86_64):** User executes `SYSCALL` instruction. Kernel entry in `entry.S` saves registers, calls same `do_ipc()`.

## System Call Path (same as MINIX 3)

```
User: read(fd, buf, count)
  |
  v
musl: read.c fills Message { m_type: VFS_READ, fd, buf_ptr, count }
  |   calls _syscall(VFS_PROC_NR, VFS_READ, &msg)
  |     calls ipc_sendrec(VFS_PROC_NR, &msg)
  |       executes SVC (aarch64) or SYSCALL (x86_64)
  v
Kernel: do_ipc() -> mini_send() copies msg to VFS deliver_msg, unblocks VFS
         -> mini_receive() blocks caller until VFS replies
  |
  v
VFS: sef_receive() returns the message
  |   dispatches to do_read()
  |   routes to MFS via REQ_READ message
  |   MFS reads from disk (via BDEV_READ to virtio-blk)
  |   MFS replies to VFS
  |   VFS replies to user process
  v
Kernel: mini_send() delivers reply, unblocks user
  |
  v
musl: _syscall() returns result, sets errno if negative
  |
  v
User: read() returns bytes read
```

## musl-libc Integration

The musl fork (v1.2.5, MIT license) needs the following changes:

**New files to add (`src/minix/`):**
- `_syscall.c` -- `int _syscall(endpoint_t who, int callnr, message *m)` using `ipc_sendrec()`
- `_ipc_aarch64.S` -- `SVC`-based IPC trap
- `_ipc_x86_64.S` -- `SYSCALL`-based IPC trap (matches kernel's `entry.S` ABI)
- ~100 POSIX wrapper files (open.c, read.c, write.c, fork.c, exit.c, etc.) that construct MINIX messages and call `_syscall()`. Structurally identical to MINIX 3's `lib/libc/sys/` wrappers.

**Files to modify:**
- `arch/aarch64/syscall_arch.h` -- Gut Linux `__syscall*` macros; redirect to MINIX path
- `arch/x86_64/syscall_arch.h` -- Same
- `Makefile` -- Add `src/minix/` sources

**Include bridge:** A small header set (`minix/ipc.h`, `minix/com.h`, `minix/callnr.h`) generated from `kernel-shared` Rust crate via `cbindgen`, so the C wrappers use the same message types and call numbers as the Rust kernel and servers.

## Boot Sequence

**Bootloader:** Limine (BSD-licensed, supports x86_64 BIOS+UEFI and aarch64 UEFI).

```
Limine loads kernel ELF64 from FAT32 boot partition
  -> _start (entry.S): set kernel stack, call kmain()
  -> kmain():
     1. Parse Limine responses (memmap, HHDM offset)
     2. Init kernel heap, serial console
     3. Unpack embedded boot image -> module_list[]
     4. arch_init() -- exception vectors, GIC, timer (aarch64) or GDT/IDT/APIC (x86_64)
     5. proc_init() -- clear process table
     6. Load each boot module ELF, create page tables, set privileges
     7. system_init() -- register kernel call handlers
     8. Enable timer interrupt
     9. Unblock boot processes
    10. switch_to_user() -- schedule first process (never returns)

Boot processes start in order:
  DS -> RS -> PM -> SCHED -> VFS -> memory -> tty -> VM -> PFS -> MFS -> init
```

Boot modules are packed into the kernel ELF as a `.boot_image` section (MXBI header + ELF entries).

## Build System

- **Cargo workspace** at root for all Rust crates (kernel, servers, drivers, userland)
- **Custom Rust targets** (`aarch64-minix-kernel.json`, `aarch64-minix-user.json`, plus x86_64 variants) for `no_std` kernel and freestanding userspace
- **musl** built separately via its own Makefile with cross-compilation flags; produces `libc.a` + `crt*.o` installed to a sysroot
- **`tools/mkbootimage.rs`** packs server/driver ELF binaries into the boot archive linked into the kernel
- **`tools/mkimage.sh`** creates GPT disk: FAT32 boot partition (Limine + kernel) + MinixFS root
- **`tools/qemu-run.sh`** launches QEMU with VirtIO devices and serial console

- `drivers/driver-rt/`: VirtIO MMIO transport (aarch64), virtqueue management, BDEV/CDEV protocol
- `drivers/virtio-blk/`: Block device
- `drivers/virtio-console/`: TTY
- `drivers/virtio-net/`: Network (packet I/O only; TCP/IP stack is later)
- Root filesystem on VirtIO disk
- **Milestone:** Boots from VirtIO disk, mounts MinixFS root

### Phase 7: Userland

- `userland/init/`: Run /etc/rc, respawn gettys
- `userland/sh/`: Simple shell (pipes, redirects, background jobs, builtins)
- `userland/coreutils/`: Multi-call binary -- ls, cat, cp, mv, rm, mkdir, rmdir, echo, wc, head, tail, grep, chmod, pwd, env, sleep, date, uname, kill, ps, true, false, test
- **Milestone:** Login, navigate filesystem, run scripts

### Phase 8: x86_64 Port

- `kernel/src/arch/x86_64/`: GDT, IDT, APIC, SYSCALL/SYSRET, 4-level page tables, context switch
- `musl/src/minix/_ipc_x86_64.S`
- VirtIO PCI transport
- `tools/qemu-run-x86_64.sh`
- **Milestone:** Same minix.rs boots on `qemu-system-x86_64`

### Phase 9: Documentation + Polish

- Comprehensive rustdoc across all crates
- Architecture guide for students
- End-to-end syscall trace walkthrough ("How read() works")
- IPC latency + context switch benchmarks
- Test suite (kernel unit tests, IPC stress, POSIX conformance)
- **Milestone:** Teaching-ready OS with documentation

---

## Key Design Decisions

**Rust kernel, not incremental port:** MINIX 3's C kernel uses raw pointers, global mutable state, and macro-heavy abstractions that resist incremental Rustification. A greenfield kernel uses proper Rust patterns from the start (enums for flags, Result for errors, indices not pointers for linked lists).

**`unsafe` boundaries in kernel:** (a) Process table access (`UnsafeCell` static array), (b) user-space memory copies, (c) hardware register access (inline asm), (d) assembly entry/exit paths. Each `unsafe` block gets a `// SAFETY:` comment.

**musl over Rust libc:** musl is well-tested, BSD-compatible, and complete. The MINIX-specific work is confined to ~100 syscall wrappers + IPC assembly stub. The rest of musl (stdio, string, math, locale) works unchanged.

**Servers in Rust:** Shared `kernel-shared` message types provide compile-time IPC protocol verification. C servers (linked against musl) also work since the IPC mechanism is language-agnostic.

**Multi-call coreutils:** Single `coreutils` binary dispatching on argv[0] (like BusyBox) minimizes disk space and simplifies building.

---

## Verification Strategy

Each phase has a concrete milestone testable in QEMU (aarch64 primary):

- Phase 0: `docs/` complete, directory tree navigable, CLAUDE.md in place
- Phase 1: `qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt` -> serial output visible
- Phase 2: Ping-pong test via IPC verified by serial trace
- Phase 3: Boot processes run in separate address spaces
- Phase 4: Server initialization sequence completes to init
- Phase 5: `printf("Hello\n")` from C program reaches serial
- Phase 6: Boots from VirtIO disk, mounts MinixFS root
- Phase 7: Interactive shell session
- Phase 8: Same tests pass on `qemu-system-x86_64`
- Phase 9: `cargo doc`, test suite green

QEMU flags for aarch64 dev:
```
qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -cpu cortex-a72 -m 256M \
  -serial stdio -no-reboot -d int,cpu_reset -D qemu.log \
  -drive file=minixrs.img,format=raw,if=virtio \
  -device virtio-net-device
```
GDB: add `-s -S` then `rust-gdb -ex "target remote :1234"`

Paths are relative to the MINIX 3 source tree root (under the `minix/` subdirectory
for MINIX-specific code). See https://github.com/Stichting-MINIX-Research-Foundation/minix

| Message definitions | `include/minix/ipc.h` |
| IPC constants | `include/minix/ipcconst.h` |
| Server endpoints + call numbers | `include/minix/com.h`, `include/minix/callnr.h` |
| User-space IPC stubs | `lib/libc/arch/x86_64/sys/_ipc.S` |
| _syscall() wrapper | `lib/libc/sys/syscall.c` |
| POSIX wrappers (template for musl) | `lib/libc/sys/*.c` |
| SEF framework | `lib/libsys/sef.c` |
| Boot process table | `kernel/table.c` |
| Limine integration design | `BOOT.md` (at repo root) |

content.text:
Reference groundwork is done. Key facts banked for the design session:

- **Grants (MINIX 3 model):** the grant table lives in the *granter's own address space*; `SYS_SETGRANT` merely records its address/size in the granter's `Priv`. At `SYS_SAFECOPY` time the kernel reads the grant entry cross-address-space and validates grantee/range/access. Three grant kinds (direct, indirect, magic) with seq-numbered grant IDs for staleness — direct grants alone likely suffice for Phase 5's VFS paths.
- **Console (MINIX 3 model):** `SYS_DIAGCTL` with `DIAGCTL_CODE_DIAG` copies a bounded user buffer into the kernel and emits it via `kputc` — a small, real kernel call that maps directly onto our existing UART writer.
- **Root image (MINIX 3 model):** a `memory` driver serving a boot-embedded ramdisk is how MINIX boots before disk drivers — which maps naturally onto our MXBI archive as the carrier.
- **VFS↔FS protocol:** MINIX 3 has ~33 `REQ_*` calls; Phase 5 needs only a small subset (mount/READSUPER, LOOKUP, PUTNODE, READ, WRITE, STAT-ish) for the hello-world milestone.

The three exploration agents (kernel internals, shared ABI + servers, musl fork state) are still running — their results determine the clarifying questions I'll ask you (console sink, root image, grant model, ELF authority, cbindgen timing, musl vendoring, plus milestone/scope). I'll pick this up as soon as they report back.

## 1. User-memory copy paths

**The entire user-copy surface is two functions**, both in `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/ipc/message.rs`:
- `copy_msg_from_user(va) -> Result<Message, i32>` — message.rs:35, a bounds check then `core::ptr::read_volatile(va as *const Message)` (message.rs:41)
- `copy_msg_to_user(va, &Message)` — message.rs:48, `write_volatile` (message.rs:54)

Both are **direct dereferences of the active TTBR0** — no HHDM walk, no cross-AS translation. There is no `copy_from_user`/`copy_to_user` for arbitrary buffers, and no cross-address-space copy helper anywhere. A grep for `read_volatile|write_volatile|copy_nonoverlapping` outside UART/GIC/MMU turns up only these two plus three *kernel-side* HHDM copies (`elf.rs:189`, `do_fork.rs:218`, `userland.rs:537`) — all of which copy into freshly-allocated frames via `phys_to_hhdm`, not into a live user AS.

**Validation** is `user_va_ok(va, len)` at `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel-shared/src/message.rs:64`: rejects `va < 8`, non-8-aligned, and `va + len > USER_VA_TOP` (`1 << 48`). It is a **pure range/alignment predicate — it does not consult the page tables.**

**Call sites:**
- Send/sendrec request read: `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/ipc/send.rs:75`
- Kernel-call request read + reply write: `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/system/mod.rs:122` and `mod.rs:141`
- Receive: stashes the VA only — `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/ipc/receive.rs:64` sets `deliver_msg_vir = user_msg_va`
- **Deferred flush:** `flush_deliver_msg(p)` at `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/ipc/mod.rs:276-286`, called from `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/proc/sched.rs:321` — **after** `switch_ttbr0_with_asid` on line 320. The ordering is load-bearing and commented at sched.rs:311: the flush writes through the newly-installed TTBR0, so it only works because the receiver's AS is already live. Result is `let _ = ...` — errors are silently dropped (mod.rs:280-284 acknowledges there's no place to signal; notes phase 3 "adds MF_MSGFAILED", which does not exist).

**Bad pointer today → kernel panic, no recovery.** The doc comment at message.rs:18-22 and :29-34 states this outright: in-range-but-unmapped VAs are expected to fault and panic. There is **no fault fixup / exception table** anywhere (`grep fixup|extable|__ex_table` in kernel/src returns nothing).

**Same-EL vectors:** `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/arch/aarch64/vectors.S`. Slots 4-7 (Current EL with SP_ELx, i.e. where an EL1 data abort from a user-copy lands) are `EXC_ENTRY el1h_sync, 4` etc. (vectors.S:80-86) — the generic macro that dumps registers and calls `exception_entry`, which is `-> !` and `panic!`s unconditionally (`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/arch/aarch64/exception.rs:54-75`). **It does not inspect ELR to see if the fault was inside a user-copy, and there is no way to return.** Only slot 8 (`el0_64_sync` → `trap.S`) and slot 9 (`el0_64_irq` → `interrupt.S`) are wired to real handlers; `do_page_fault` (exception.rs:148) is EL0-only and explicitly bails to `el0_sync_unexpected` for any EC other than 0x20/0x24, and also for permission faults (exception.rs:176-178).

So for Phase 5: a fault-recovering copy needs (a) a real `el1h_sync` handler, (b) an ELR fixup table or a "current copy in progress" per-CPU marker, and (c) an `MF_MSGFAILED`-equivalent to report the failure back.

## 2. Kernel call surface

Numbers: `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel-shared/src/callnr.rs`, `KERNEL_CALL = 0x600` (callnr.rs:11). All 18 exist as numbers:

| # | call | line | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| +0 | SYS_GETINFO | :14 | **real** (`do_getinfo.rs`, GET_WHOAMI only) |
| +1 | SYS_PRIVCTL | :15 | **real** (4.5) |
| +2 | SYS_FORK | :16 | **real** (4.6) |
| +3 | SYS_EXEC | :24 | **real** (4.7) |
| +4 | SYS_EXIT | :25 | **real** (4.5) |
| +5 | **SYS_COPY** | :26 | **ENOSYS stub** |
| +6 | **SYS_SAFECOPY** | :27 | **ENOSYS stub** |
| +7 | **SYS_IRQCTL** | :28 | **ENOSYS stub** |
| +8 | SYS_VMCTL | :29 | **real** (3.3) |
| +9 | SYS_SCHEDULE | :30 | **real** (4.3) |
| +10 | SYS_SETALARM | :31 | **real** (4.4) |
| +11 | **SYS_TIMES** | :32 | **ENOSYS stub** |
| +12 | **SYS_DIAGCTL** | :33 | **ENOSYS stub** |
| +13 | **SYS_SETGRANT** | :34 | **ENOSYS stub** |
| +14 | SYS_SCHEDCTL | :40 | **real** |
| +15 | SYS_KILL | :47 | **real** (4.5) |
| +16 | SYS_GETKSIG | :53 | **real** |
| +17 | SYS_ENDKSIG | :56 | **real** |

All six stubs are one-line `ENOSYS` macros in `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/system/stubs.rs:25-38`.

**Dispatch** (`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/system/mod.rs`):
- Entry `kernel_call_sendrec` (mod.rs:91) — SENDREC-to-SYSTEM fast path, diverted from `ipc::dispatch` (mod.rs:179-188 of ipc/mod.rs). Checks `ipc_to` bit for SYSTEM (mod.rs:115-120), copies request in, stamps `m_source` with the verified caller endpoint (mod.rs:130), dispatches, writes reply back to the same VA.
- `kernel_call_dispatch` (mod.rs:171) — range-checks `m_type - KERNEL_CALL` against `NR_SYS_CALLS`, gates on `k_call_mask` (mod.rs:188), then **two arms**:
  - **target-taking** match at mod.rs:194-206 — gets `&mut [Proc; N_PROC_SLOTS]` + `&mut [Priv]` + `caller_nr`: VMCTL, SCHEDULE, SCHEDCTL, KILL, GETKSIG, ENDKSIG, EXIT, FORK, EXEC, PRIVCTL (10 calls). Target resolution via `resolve_target` (mod.rs:65).

**Sizing:** `NR_KERN_CALLS_PHASE4 = 18` (callnr.rs:72), `NR_SYS_CALLS = 32` (callnr.rs:77, asserted `>= NR_KERN_CALLS_PHASE4` and multiple-of-32). `K_CALL_MASK_CHUNKS = NR_SYS_CALLS / 32 = 1` (`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/proc/priv_struct.rs:28`) — so `k_call_mask` is a single `u32` today. **14 free call slots before the mask needs a second word.**

**Who gets what:** `SRV_T` privs get `fill_bits(&mut pr.k_call_mask, NR_KERN_CALLS_PHASE4)` — all 18 (`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/proc/table.rs:485`). The shared USER priv gets `k_call_mask.fill(0)` — **zero kernel calls**, `trap_mask = USR_T`, `ipc_to = {PM}` only (table.rs:410-413). init runs on the USER priv (table.rs:454-462).

## 3. ELF loader

`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/boot_image/elf.rs`:
- **Interface:** `pub fn load_into(elf: &[u8], aspace: &mut AddrSpace) -> Result<u64, ElfError>` (elf.rs:90) — returns `e_entry`. **Input is a plain byte slice; it does not care where the bytes came from.** All field reads are explicit `from_le_bytes` (elf.rs:70-86) precisely because the input carries no alignment guarantee (elf.rs:13-15).
- **Assumptions:** `ET_EXEC` only (elf.rs:103, `BadType`), ELFCLASS64 + LSB + EM_AARCH64, `e_phentsize == 56`. Per segment: **`p_vaddr` AND `p_offset` must both be 4 KiB-aligned** and `p_filesz <= p_memsz` (elf.rs:148, `Misaligned`); `p_offset + p_filesz <= elf.len()`; **W^X enforced** (elf.rs:162, `WriteExec`). No PIE/ET_DYN, no relocations, no PT_INTERP, no PT_TLS handling, no `p_align` respect beyond page.
- **Mapping:** one `alloc_frame()` per page of `p_memsz`, copy via `phys_to_hhdm`, `flush_icache_range` if executable, `aspace.map_page` (elf.rs:172-197). BSS is free because frames are zeroed on hand-out.

Wrapper: `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/arch/aarch64/userland.rs:339` — `pub(crate) unsafe fn load_exec_image(elf: &[u8]) -> Option<ExecImage>`; `ExecImage { ttbr0_pa, asid, entry, sp_top }` (userland.rs:319-324). Builds `AddrSpace::new()`, loads, maps **exactly one** RW stack page at `SERVER_STACK_VA`, allocates an ASID, `mem::forget`s the AddrSpace. On any failure it runs `destroy_addrspace_with_leaves` (userland.rs:389) so nothing leaks. **`sp_top = SERVER_STACK_VA + PAGE_SIZE` — a single 4 KiB stack, no argv/envp/auxv construction at all.**

`SYS_EXEC` (`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/system/do_exec.rs:71`): payload is `[0..4] = target endpoint`, `[4..4+EXEC_NAME_LEN] = NUL-padded name`. It resolves the name via `BootImage::get().module_by_name(name)` (do_exec.rs:106) which returns a `&'static [u8]` into the `include_bytes!`-embedded MXBI archive (`/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/boot_image/mod.rs:34, :113`). Rejects `SELF`/caller (active-TTBR0 hazard), requires target be a clean `RTS_RECEIVING` blocked receiver with no `MF_DELIVERMSG` (do_exec.rs:116). Loads new image first (untouched-on-failure), then swaps, tears down old AS via `do_exit::teardown_addrspace`, `rts_unset(RTS_RECEIVING)`.

**Could it load ELF bytes from a user-space server?** The loader itself, yes — it takes `&[u8]` and makes no static-lifetime demand. What's missing:
1. **A way to get the bytes.** There is no bulk user→kernel copy. You'd need `SYS_SAFECOPY`/grants or a VM-mapped shared buffer, plus the fault-recovering copy from §1.
2. **Kernel-side staging.** No kernel heap (`no_std`, no allocator visible) — you'd need to stage into frames from `mm::alloc_frame` and hand `load_into` a slice over the HHDM alias, or teach it a chunked/reader interface.
3. **Hardening.** Today `ElfError` variants are documented as "all fatal at boot (the embedded VM ELF is produced by our own build, so any of these means a build/loader bug)" (elf.rs:23-24) — the checks exist and are sound, but a hostile-input review is warranted (notably `e_phoff + i*56` arithmetic is checked only by `rd_*`'s slice `get`, which is fine, and `p_memsz.div_ceil(PAGE_SIZE)` has no cap → a huge `p_memsz` is a frame-exhaustion DoS, bounded only by `alloc_frame` returning `None`).
4. `ET_EXEC` + `p_offset` page-alignment means musl-produced binaries need `-static` and a linker script matching `servers/*/user.ld`; a stock musl static link will usually satisfy `ET_EXEC` but **not necessarily the `p_offset` page-alignment requirement** — that's the likeliest breakage.
5. The `SYS_EXEC` payload carries a 16-byte name, not a pointer/length — the message ABI would need a new sub-form.

## 4. Console output

- `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/uart.rs` is 9 lines: `pub use crate::arch::Uart;`.
- Backend `/Users/kevinbarnard/src/minixrs/kernel/src/arch/aarch64/uart.rs`: `Pl011` at phys `0x0900_0000` (uart.rs:24), reached via HHDM; `set_base(virt)` called once from `main.rs:45`. `putc` polls `FR.TXFF` then writes `DR`; **drops bytes silently if base is 0** (uart.rs:48-50). `impl fmt::Write` does LF→CRLF (uart.rs:64-74).
- **There are no `print!`/`println!`/`kprint!` macros.** Every site is `writeln!(Uart::new(), ...)` or `writeln!(Pl011::new(), ...)`. `Uart::new()` is stateless (just reloads the atomic base), so it's constructed ad-hoc everywhere. Adding a macro layer is a clean, low-risk Phase 5 nicety.
- **There is no user/server path to the console. None.** `SYS_DIAGCTL` exists as number `KERNEL_CALL+12` and is dispatched (mod.rs:234) but returns `ENOSYS` (stubs.rs:37). Grepping all of `servers/`, `drivers/`, `userland/`, `server-rt/`, `minix-ipc/` for `uart|Uart|PL011|0x0900_0000` returns **zero hits**, and for `DIAGCTL|SYS_COPY|SAFECOPY|SETGRANT|SYS_TIMES|IRQCTL` also **zero hits**. Servers are observable only through kernel-emitted traces (`[ksys N]` at mod.rs:149, `[pf]` at exception.rs:211, per-call traces in `do_exec.rs:169` etc.).
- `drivers/virtio-console/src/main.rs` is a 5-line placeholder. `servers/vfs/src/main.rs` is 80 lines; `fs/mfs`, `fs/pfs`, `userland/sh`, `userland/coreutils` are all 5-line stubs.

So **`SYS_DIAGCTL` is the natural first Phase 5 deliverable** — it's already numbered, already in the `k_call_mask` (SRV_T gets all 18), already routed to a caller-local arm with the right signature, and needs only a body. ### `error.rs` — **the musl bridge's biggest ABI risk**
Present: `OK 0`, `EGENERIC -1`, `EPERM -2`, `ENOENT -3`, `ESRCH -4`, `EINTR -5`, `EIO -6`, `ENXIO -7`, `E2BIG -8`, `ENOEXEC -9`, `EBADF -10`, `ECHILD -11`, `EAGAIN -12`, `ENOMEM -13`, `EACCES -14`, **`EFAULT -15`**, `EINVAL -21`, `EDEADLK -29`, **`ENOSYS -44`**; IPC block `ELOCKED -101` … **`EDEADSRCDST -105`** … `EDONTREPLY -109` (`error.rs:9-41`).

Missing and needed by any FS: `EEXIST`, `EISDIR`, `ENOTDIR`, `ENOTEMPTY`, `ENOSPC`, `EMFILE`, `ENFILE`, `EXDEV`, `EROFS`, `ESPIPE`, `EPIPE`, `ENAMETOOLONG`, `ELOOP`, `EBUSY`, `ENODEV`, `ENOTTY`, `EMLINK`, `EFBIG`, `ERANGE`, `EDOM`.

**Numbering caveat worth an explicit design decision:** the header claims "Values match MINIX 3 `include/minix/errno.h`" (`error.rs:6`), but the first block is uniformly *one greater in magnitude* than POSIX/Linux (`EPERM -2` vs 1, `EFAULT -15` vs 14) while later values don't follow that offset (`EINVAL -21` vs 22, `EDEADLK -29` vs 35, `ENOSYS -44` vs 38). Whatever the intent, these must be reconciled against real MINIX 3 values *before* cbindgen emits `<errno.h>` for musl — musl's own errno tables assume Linux numbering.

### C-friendliness / cbindgen readiness
**Clean:**
- `Message` — `#[repr(C, align(8))]`, three POD fields. Emits perfectly.
- `Endpoint`/`GenNr` are `pub type … = i32` (`endpoint.rs:26,29`) → plain typedefs.
- `callnr.rs`, `error.rs`, `ipc_const.rs`, `signal.rs`, `sys_limits.rs` — all plain `i32`/`usize` consts, at most simple arithmetic on other consts (`KERNEL_CALL + 3`). cbindgen handles these.
- No generics, no `Option` in public data types, no enums-with-data anywhere in `kernel-shared`.

**Will choke / needs config:**
- `ProcNr` and `PrivId` are `#[repr(transparent)]` newtypes (`endpoint.rs:38-40, 63-65`) with `const fn new/get` and `impl Display`. cbindgen emits a wrapper struct unless you configure transparent→typedef.

## 5. MXBI boot archive + adding a module

### `kernel/build.rs`
- Servers array at `build.rs:128-137`: `[(&str, PathBuf, i32); 8]` — **fixed-size array, must bump the length to add anything.** Order matters: VM first (takes ASID 1, blocks on `RECEIVE(ANY)` immediately). Current rows: `vm 7, ds 5, vfs 1, sched 9, rs 2, pm 0, init 10, worker -1`.
- **Proc numbers are hardcoded integer literals with `// VM_PROC_NR`-style comments** — build.rs can't depend on `kernel-shared`, so this is an unguarded drift surface. Adding `mfs 6` / `memory 3` means duplicating those literals correctly.
- `build_server` (`:173-226`) builds each crate with a *nested* cargo invocation: `--target aarch64-unknown-none --release`, isolated `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS = -Clink-arg=-T<crate>/user.ld` (which *replaces* the workspace's kernel linker-script rustflags). Every new server therefore needs its own `user.ld` and pays a full nested build on every kernel build.
- `rerun-if-changed` covers `minix-ipc/src`, `server-rt/src`, `kernel-shared/src` as directories (`:115-121`) plus each crate's `src/`, `user.ld`, `Cargo.toml` (`:187-193`).

### `pack_mxbi` (`build.rs:238-278`) — record format
```
header 16B: magic 0x4942584D "MXBI" | version=1 | entry_count:u32 | total_size:u32
record 32B × N: proc_nr:i32 | offset:u32 | len:u32 | name:[u8;20]
payloads back-to-back at recorded offsets
```
All fields little-endian. Name must be `< 20` bytes (asserted `:253-256`). Signature is `&[(i32, String, Vec<u8>)]`.

### **Can a non-ELF blob be packed?** — Yes, with no format change.
1. `pack_mxbi` takes opaque `Vec<u8>` and does **zero** content validation (`build.rs:238-278`).
2. `BootImage::get()` validates only magic/version/table-bounds and per-record `offset + len <= bytes.len()` (`boot_image/mod.rs:53-77`) — never touches payload content.
3. The boot loader **explicitly skips negative `proc_nr`**: `kernel/src/arch/aarch64/userland.rs:184-190` — `if nr.get() < 0 { continue; }`, comment cites `com::EXEC_ONLY_PROC_NR`. So a module tagged `-1` is never ELF-parsed at boot.
4. `BootImage::module_by_name(&str) -> Option<&'static [u8]>` (`mod.rs:113-119`) returns **raw bytes with no ELF check**. Only `do_exec.rs:106` feeds the result to `elf::load_into`, which is where `ElfError::BadMagic/BadClass/BadType` (`boot_image/elf.rs:29-40`) would fire.

So an initramfs / MFS disk image can be packed today as `("initramfs", bytes, -1)` and retrieved by name. Constraints to design around:
- The whole archive is `include_bytes!`'d into kernel `.rodata` (`mod.rs:34`), landing in Limine's `EXECUTABLE_AND_MODULES` region — **never freed, and it inflates the kernel binary 1:1** with the image size. A multi-MiB FS image is a real cost.
- `offset`/`len` are `u32` → 4 GiB cap (fine).
- `build_server` assumes every module is a cargo crate; a raw blob needs a separate `std::fs::read` path in `build_boot_image`.
- Name field is 20 bytes NUL-padded, but `EXEC_NAME_LEN = 16` (`callnr.rs:66`) bounds what `SYS_EXEC` can carry — a longer blob name is reachable only from kernel-internal callers.
- Consider whether the FS image should instead be a Limine module (separate file, not embedded) — nothing in the current design forecloses that, but nothing supports it either.

```
header 16B: magic 0x4942584D "MXBI" | version=1 | entry_count:u32 | total_size:u32

```
All fields little-endian. Name must be `< 20` bytes (asserted `:253-256`). Signature is `&[(i32, String, Vec<u8>)]`.

### **Can a non-ELF blob be packed?** — Yes, with no format change.
1. `pack_mxbi` takes opaque `Vec<u8>` and does **zero** content validation (`build.rs:238-278`).
2. `BootImage::get()` validates only magic/version/table-bounds and per-record `offset + len <= bytes.len()` (`boot_image/mod.rs:53-77`) — never touches payload content.

- `offset`/`len` are `u32` → 4 GiB cap (fine).
- `build_server` assumes every module is a cargo crate; a raw blob needs a separate `std::fs::read` path in `build_boot_image`.
- Name field is 20 bytes NUL-padded, but `EXEC_NAME_LEN = 16` (`callnr.rs:66`) bounds what `SYS_EXEC` can carry — a longer blob name is reachable only from kernel-internal callers.

questions.question: Console/stdio sink for the printf milestone: how should bytes reach the serial console? Context: SYS_DIAGCTL already exists as a numbered, mask-granted, dispatch-routed ENOSYS stub — it only needs a body. MINIX 3's model is exactly this (bounded buffer → kernel → kputc). A real TTY driver is Phase 6 (virtio-console).

options.label: SYS_DIAGCTL kernel call (Recommended)
options.description: Make the existing stub real: servers pass text to the kernel, kernel writes to PL011 UART. User programs' write(1/2) routes user→VFS→SYS_DIAGCTL. Inline 96-byte message chunks work before any copy machinery exists; MINIX 3's exact pre-TTY model. TTY server stays Phase 6.

options.label: Minimal TTY server now
options.description: Stand up the TTY proc (slot 4 already exists) with an EL0 PL011 driver: needs MMIO mapping into user space + IRQ routing — pulls Phase 6 driver infrastructure into Phase 5.

options.label: Defer (kernel traces only)
options.description: No user-visible console in Phase 5; printf milestone proven only via kernel-side traces. Weakest milestone.

questions.question: Root-image strategy: where does the root filesystem live before block drivers exist? Context: the MXBI boot archive can already carry a non-ELF blob (negative proc_nr entries are skipped by the boot loader, retrievable by name), and the MEM proc slot (3) already exists kernel-side. MINIX 3 boots from a ramdisk served by its `memory` driver.

options.label: MFS image + memory driver (Recommended)
options.description: Pack an MFS-formatted image into MXBI; kernel maps it read-only into the memory driver's address space at boot; memory driver serves it over a minimal BDEV protocol to MFS. Exactly the MINIX shape — Phase 6 swaps in virtio-blk with zero MFS changes. Needs a host-side mkfs tool (Rust, host-tested, sharing MFS's on-disk structs).

options.label: MFS reads image directly
options.description: Kernel maps the image into MFS itself; MFS skips BDEV and reads memory directly. One less server + protocol in Phase 5, but MFS needs rework when real block devices arrive in Phase 6.

options.label: Initramfs unpacked by VFS
options.description: A cpio-like archive VFS unpacks into an in-memory FS. Avoids MFS entirely — but MFS is the Phase 5 deliverable, so this replaces the goal rather than serving it.

questions.question: Grant model for cross-address-space data movement (every FS data path needs it). Context: Priv already has unused grant_table/grant_entries fields; SYS_SETGRANT/SYS_SAFECOPY/SYS_COPY are all ENOSYS stubs. The chunk-6 spec says 'prefer real grants'. Key insight from exploration: copies done by explicit page-table walk via HHDM are inherently fault-safe (unmapped page = lookup miss → EFAULT, no exception handling needed).

options.label: Real grants: direct+magic, + SYS_COPY (Recommended)
options.description: MINIX-style grant table in the granter's address space; SYS_SETGRANT registers it; SYS_SAFECOPY validates + copies via HHDM page-table walks. Direct grants (server↔server) and magic grants (VFS grants MFS access to a user's buffer — the real read/write data path, single copy). Plus SYS_COPY as the privileged raw copy MINIX VFS also uses. Indirect grants deferred.

options.label: Real grants: direct only
options.description: Direct grants only; VFS double-copies user data through its own buffers (user→VFS via SYS_COPY, VFS→MFS via direct grant). Simpler verify_grant, but the FS data path is a double copy and magic grants get retrofitted later anyway.

options.label: Interim kernel copy API only
options.description: Just SYS_COPY (raw privileged endpoint+addr copy), no grant table. Fastest to build, but every byte moves ungoverned — and the chunk-6 spec explicitly prefers real grants.

questions.question: ELF-loading authority for FS-backed exec: who parses and maps the binary when exec sources from the filesystem? Context: kernel boot_image/elf.rs takes a plain byte slice (source-agnostic, W^X-enforcing); plan.md promised 'Phase 5 swaps the exec source to a VFS file with no PM/kernel rework'. The kernel has no heap, so it can't stage a whole file — but elf.rs can be refactored over a chunked-reader source.

options.label: Kernel stays authority, grant source (Recommended)
options.description: PM/VFS stage the file in user space; SYS_EXEC gains a payload form carrying a grant to the image; elf.rs reads headers/segments through cross-AS grant reads (page-at-a-time, same copy engine as safecopy). Reuses the hardened loader, no kernel staging memory, minimal PM change.

options.label: User-space loader (VM/PM)
options.description: MINIX-authentic direction (VFS/libexec parse ELF, VM maps segments): but requires exposing map-into-third-party-AS through SYS_VMCTL and duplicating the loader in user space — a much bigger lift for the same milestone.

questions.question: TTY server scope for Phase 5: what's the minimal shape? Context: only TX is needed for the printf milestone (polling the PL011 needs no IRQs; RX/input is naturally Phase 6-7 territory alongside virtio-console and the shell). The server needs the UART's MMIO page (phys 0x0900_0000) mapped into its EL0 address space somehow — today AddrSpace only maps normal RAM frames, so device mappings (Device-nGnRE attributes) are new either way.

options.label: TX-only, boot-premapped MMIO (Recommended)
options.description: Kernel pre-maps the UART page into TTY's address space at boot (TTY is a boot server; one-off, like stack setup). TTY polls FR/writes DR. VFS routes fd 1/2 over a CDEV band with grants; TTY safecopies and writes. No IRQ work, no new VMCTL subcall. RX + IRQs come with Phase 6.

options.label: TX-only, VM-mediated map_phys
options.description: Add a VMCTL_MAP_PHYS subcall so TTY requests the device mapping through VM at init — more MINIX-authentic (drivers mmap device memory via VM), reusable for virtio-mmio in Phase 6, but +1 kernel/VM surface now.

options.label: TX + RX with IRQ routing
options.description: Full console: SYS_IRQCTL made real, GIC routes UART RX to an EL0 notification. Significant kernel work (IRQ hook framework) that nothing in Phase 5 consumes — input has no reader until a shell exists.

questions.question: Errno strategy: error.rs must be reconciled before C headers freeze. Verified state: our values are bespoke (EPERM −2, EINVAL −21, ENOSYS −44 — the 'matches MINIX 3' comment is wrong); classic book-era MINIX numbering (EPERM 1 … EINVAL 22, EDEADLK 35, ENOSYS 38) is IDENTICAL to Linux/musl numbering for the POSIX block; modern MINIX switched to NetBSD numbering (EAGAIN 35, ENOSYS 78, IPC errnos at 202+).

options.label: Classic-MINIX/Linux values (Recommended)
options.description: Renumber error.rs: POSIX block takes the classic-MINIX values (= musl's stock bits/errno.h, so strerror and every macro work unmodified), MINIX IPC errnos (ELOCKED, EDEADSRCDST…) move above 200 like modern MINIX to stay clear of Linux's range. Both authentic AND zero musl translation. One mechanical renumber PR, host tests catch stragglers.

options.label: Keep bespoke + translate in musl
options.description: Leave error.rs as-is; the musl _syscall wrapper carries a MINIX→musl errno mapping table forever. No kernel churn now, permanent translation layer + two numbering systems to reason about.

options.label: NetBSD numbering (modern MINIX)
options.description: Adopt modern MINIX/NetBSD values (EAGAIN 35, ENOSYS 78) and override musl's bits/errno.h to match. Most faithful to the modern reference tree, but every errno diverges from Linux muscle memory and musl needs a full bits override.

questions.question: C header bridge (minix/ipc.h, com.h, callnr.h for musl wrappers): generation mechanism and timing? Context: Message is repr(C)-clean, but com.rs endpoint constants are ProcNr::new() calls that cbindgen cannot const-evaluate — it would skip or mangle them. Chunk-6 asks for the freeze timing; the natural point is the slice where the first C file lands.

options.label: Hand-rolled generator tool (Recommended)
options.description: A small host binary (tools/ crate) that depends on kernel-shared as a normal Rust dep and prints the C headers — 100% value-accurate by construction (no const-eval limits), CI check reruns it and fails on drift. Freeze ABI + generate in the slice that starts musl work.

options.label: cbindgen + mirror consts
options.description: Add plain-i32 mirror constants beside every ProcNr::new() and configure cbindgen's transparent-newtype handling. Standard tooling, but duplicates every constant and adds a config surface that must track future types.

options.label: Hand-written headers + drift test
options.description: Write the ~3 headers by hand once, plus a host test asserting each C value equals the Rust constant. Least tooling, most manual upkeep as the ABI grows.

questions.question: musl vendoring policy: how does the musl fork enter the build? Context: the fork lives at github (your fork of musl v1.2.5+102, MIT-clean, zero MINIX changes yet); ~11 MB working tree, 1537 C files. Sonar already excludes external/**; cargo-deny/geiger only see the cargo graph so a C tree is invisible to them either way.

options.label: Git submodule at external/musl (Recommended)
options.description: Submodule pinned to the fork's main branch. Keeps 1537 C files out of minixrs history, Sonar-excluded for free, CI checks it out only in the musl job, local dev can point at the existing ~/src/learn/musl-minix checkout. MINIX changes land as normal PRs in the fork repo.

options.label: Vendor the tree in-repo
options.description: Copy the fork under external/musl/ as tracked files. Single-repo simplicity, atomic cross-cutting PRs — at the cost of ~11 MB + 1537 C files in this repo and a manual upstream-sync story.

options.label: Build-time fetch, pinned commit
options.description: build script or CI step clones the fork at a pinned SHA into target/. No repo weight, but network-dependent builds and the pin lives in a script instead of git metadata.
